nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Striped Mullet
Scientific Name: Mugil cephalus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: Perciformes
	Family: Mugilidae

Other Common Names: Common mullet, black mullet, Biloxi bacon, liza, grey mullet (70 74 116 211 394), jumping mullet (315 834), fatback (315).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Comprises one of the most important fisheries of the southern United States with total Atlantic mullet landings for 1988 totaling over 32 million pounds (11 513 788).  Since the 1960's, Florida has produced about 80-90% of the US catch.  Statewide Florida landings for 1989 totaled 19,985,200 lbs worth $8,610,461 dockside (average $0.43/lb), of which 17,787,960 lbs were landed at Florida west coast ports (902).  State wide landings of all mullet species combined amounted to 22,798,999 lbs in 1991 (1329).  Striped mullet is considered as both an important food fish especially in Florida where it is also taken for its roe, considered a delicacy, and as a prime species for mariculture (53 116 74).  Florida roe season landings and prices were down from the previous year in 1990_91, but the 1991-92 roe season started strongly in the fall with prices reaching as high as $1.55/lb (1329).  Mullet are caught by gill nets, trammel nets, stop nets, haul seines, yard seines, hook and line, and cast nets (11 74 76 791).  The gill nets and trammel nets are the most effective means of capture with haul and yard seine second in choice.  Hook and line, and cast net catches are incidental.  About 25% is marketed fresh, 63% frozen in the round, 6% smoked, and 6% as roe (1317).

Recreational: Valued as a bait fish by sport fishermen especially for billfish, also indirectly important as an important food source for game fishes (19 377 1317).  Regarded as an excellent food fish (1317).

Indicator: A study by the Environmental Protection Agency has shown that crude oil may serve as a nonspecific stress agent that lowers resistance of mullet to disease (475).  Striped mullet responses to DDT at different temperatures have application for the development of water quality criteria in Australia (570).

Ecological Role: An important forage fish which forms a major component in the flow of energy through the estuarine system by feeding at the lowest trophic levels and providing food to birds, mammals and many important commercial and game fish (220 377 490 967 1317).  Piscine predators include: Sciaenops ocellatus, Cynoscion nebulosus, Arius felis, Paralichthys lethostigma, Carcharhinus leucas, Lepisosteus spatula, L. osseus, Megalops atlanticus (70 163 255 651).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Nearly worldwide in warm waters (788 1316).  In the western Atlantic from Nova Scotia and Bermuda to Santos, Brazil (327 788 891), but most common from the Chesapeake Bay south (1037).  Absent from the West Indies and Caribbean (788).  Found throughout the Gulf of Mexico (891).  Often ascends coastal rivers for considerable distances (790 1037).

Within study area:  Abundant along the Florida coast (1316).  Also occurs in Lake Okeechobee (1313), the St. Lucie, St. Johns and Caloosahatchee Rivers (264 265 1015), and the Big Cypress Swamp and Everglades (395).  It is found throughout the IRL system (848 887 993 264 1242)

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
All stages are pelagic occurring primarily in the shallow part of the water column although some deep water catches have been reported (18 211 327 438 754).  Larvae are planktonic until 10_12 d from hatching and are then capable of sustained swimming (394).  Prejuveniles, juveniles, and adults are nektonic and form schools ranging from a few individuals up to several hundred (18 19 65 327 377).  Activity related to feeding has been recorded during both day and night (163 301 702).
Movements and Migrations:  One tagging study showed that 91% of the tagged mullet were recovered within 32 km of the release point and only 2% were recovered more than 160 km away (1317).  Later tagging studies, however, reported extensive movements of subadult and adult mullet (>250mm TL) in Florida (1331).  Recaptures ranged from a few km to 500km from the tagging site, and one fish tagged on the Gulf Coast was recaptured in the Atlantic about 210km from the tagging site (1331).  Similar distances have been reported in Australia (1325), and distances of up to 560km have been reported on the east coast of the US (1332).  Schools have been reported to migrate around southern FL from the Atlantic to the Gulf coast (Jacot, 1920 cited in (1322)).  Mullet attain a swimming speed greater than energetically optimal during migration probably due to increased hydromechanical efficiency provided by schooling (1322) suggesting that dispersal can be rapid.

It was thought that Florida Gulf coast populations were divided into at least 3 geographic subpopulations (74 1317).  Recent analysis of electrophoretically detected allozymes was used to describe the genetic structure of Florida mullet populations (1332).  Based on these studies, it was found that striped mullet inhabiting both coasts of Florida essentially represent a single gene pool, and that the earlier speculations and interpretations of population structure could not be supported (1332).

Striped mullet exhibit an inshore-offshore movement in the fall and winter when large schools leave the bays and estuaries in order to spawn in offshore Gulf waters (74 327 481 754).  Tagging studies conducted in the Tampa Bay area indicated that 9 - 17% of tagged mullet emigrated permanently from the bay systems where they were tagged (1315 1316).  Mullet exhibit a preference for bay waters and it has been suggested an organic compound present in these waters may guide mullet back to their native area (390).  Larvae move inshore to shallow waters along beaches and salt marshes (1317), and in Hawaii, schools of mullet <50mm are always found in waters of minimal depth (1319).  Juveniles entering bay systems from offshore waters migrate to nursery areas which are thought to be secondary and tertiary bays and move back to deeper offshore waters as sub-adult to mature and spawn when colder temperatures set in (298).  Movement of mullet is otherwise random and usually restricted to a broad coastal area (74 75 76 481).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: One of the most abundant fishes in shallow Gulf waters usually with highest biomass (294). They are most abundant in waters near shore occupying virtually all shallow marine and estuarine habitats including open beaches, flats, lagoons, bays, rivers, salt marshes, and grass beds (70 103 116 255 294 298 224 255 377 550 490 588 664 694).  Eggs and larvae occupy an offshore marine habitat where they undergo early development and as prejuveniles enter the bays and estuaries to mature when 15 to 32 mm TL from November to June with the greatest concentration from December to February (255 588 294 322 224 550 694 116 696 305 709 754 510).  In some instances, females greatly outnumber males in brackish and freshwater habitats (1323 1329).  Reported from fresh to hypersaline waters and from waters with depths of a few centimeters to 1385 m appearing to prefer <3 (18 70 103 116 140 211 255 264 265 298 395 438 490 550 561 651 694 754 790).

Substrate: Prefer softer sediments such as mud and sand which contain decaying organic detritus, but also occur over finely ground shell, clay, mud and sand mixtures, silt, and silt-clay mixtures (70 140 224 377 694 702 754).  Striped mullet also frequent grass beds of Thallasia especially at night (53 298 786) and have also been observed around patches of Ruppia (224).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Egg: Egg development has been recorded over a range of 10 to 31.9 C in both laboratory and field observations with the optimum range occurring at 21 to 24 C (211 394 501 698 699 754).
Larvae: Development possible from 15.9 to 29.1 C with optimum growth and survival occurring at 20 to 22 C (394 501 698 754).  Survival and growth over a broad thermal range despite temperatures at spawning sites probably varying very little may be a preadaptation to accommodate temperatures changes as the larvae sink vertically through the water (698).
Prejuveniles occur at temperatures of 5.0 C up to a maximum exceeding 30 C (116 438 754).
Juveniles/Adults: Appear able to adjust to a wide range of temperatures (70 754).  Not a permanent resident in waters with temperatures below 16 C or where water temperatures don't reach 18 C (1317).  Recorded collections from 5.9 to 37.0 C but the ability to withstand short periods of 40 C has been observed (255 377 294 224 550 694 193 490 561 709 754).  Collected in Tampa Bay at temperatures of 10.7 - 32.5 C (664).  Preference temperatures are 20 to 30 C for juveniles and >16 to 30 C for adults (754).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Eggs: Spawning and development have occurred at 28 to 36.5 ppt with optimum survival occurring at 30 to 33 ppt (211 394 698 754).  Eggs have much less tolerance to salinity variation than larvae, but a greater tolerance to sea water (698).

Larvae: Stenohaline at hatching becoming increasingly euryhaline with increasing size (510).  Able to tolerate salinities ranging from 16 to 36.5 ppt with reported optimal ranges being 32 to 33 ppt and 26 to 28 ppt (211 394 510 698 754).  Prejuveniles recorded from a range of 0 to 54 ppt with a preference for <1 to 40 ppt (116 255 694 754).

Juvenile/Adult: Both stages euryhaline with similar tolerances; observed in salinities ranging from 0.0 to 75 ppt, but  adults appear to prefer median salinities of approximately 26 ppt  and juveniles range from 20 to 28 ppt (255 377 651 321 588 294 550 193 116 696 561 709 211 754 140).  Taken in Tampa Bay at salinities ranging from 0 to 35 ppt (664).

Other: Eggs and larvae prefer higher concentrations of oxygen (>4.0 ppm) and are not able to tolerate ranges as low as juveniles and adults can (103 754).  Larvae apparently cannot survive in dissolved oxygen concentrations below 4 ppm (1324).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Sexual, gonochoristic, polygamous, oviparous, broadcast spawners with external fertilization.

Mating/Spawning: Spawning begins in October, peaked in November-December, and ends in March (65 255 74 582 11 18 75 19 116 751 490 614 206 211 754).  Some females in Australia spawn only in alternate years (1325), and there is evidence that this may also be true for US waters (1323).  Ripe mullet collect in passes in large schools and migrate offshore with return of spent adults beginning 10 days later and continuing until May (18 255 327 490 614 1315 1316).  Spawning takes place in offshore marine waters of the Gulf of Mexico over a broad area of the continental shelf (11 18 211 298 510).  Spawners occur in small groups of 3 to 6 fish swimming close to the surface in an erratic manner (18).  Males would stay slightly behind a single female pressing against her and from time to time would visibly quiver (18 65).  No direct evidence on spawning salinities and temperatures is available, but spawning is apparently unsuccessful at low salinities (116 438).  Hormonal and natural spawning in the laboratory was best induced at 23.8 to 23.5 C and 21 C respectively (394 698) in salinities ranging from 30 to 32 ppt (394 501 698).

Fecundity: Fecundity has been estimated in laboratory studies as being 648 +/- 62 (501) to 849 +/- 62 eggs/g body weight (640) with recorded releases ranging from 0.76 to 7.2 million eggs/female (438 754).  Another study estimated fecundity is 0.5 to 2.0 million eggs/female, depending on the size of the female (74).  Fertilization rates in the laboratory have ranged from 53 to 95 % (394 501 640).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg: Non-adhesive, spherical, transparent to straw colored (438 754).  Sizes range in diameter from 0.88 to 0.94 mm and average 0.93 to 0.95 mm (211 394 501 640 698).  Characterized by a single large oil globule with a uniform diameter ranging 0.30 to 0.36 mm and averaging 0.33 mm (211 394 501).  First cleavage occurs 50 to 65 min after fertilization (AF) at 22 C; blastula stage is reached at 5 hr and 40 min AF at 24 C followed by the gastrula stage 7 hr 35 min AF (394 501).  By 13 hr 30 min AF the neurula stage occurs characterized by the appearance of the neural groove and is followed by optic vesicle development, tail expansion, somatic segmentation, and differentiation of olfactory lobes (394).  Heart beat begins 25 h 10 min AF and body movement evident at 27 h AF (394).  Incubation period is 36 to 38 hrs AF at 24 C and 48 to 50 hrs at 22 C (394 501).

Larvae: TL at hatching is 2.1 mm to 2.88 mm TL with a reported average of 2.65 +/- 0.23 mm TL (211 394 501 698).  At hatching yolk sac ovoid or oblong ellipsoidal with oil globule near center or rear of yolk sac (438).  Mouth opens on day 2 to 3; larval are independently active; eyes sufficiently pigmented for food finding; yolk sac is absorbed by day 5 (24 C) (394 501 754).  Most growth during yolksac stage occurs during day 1 with larval TL's increasing from 2.65 +/-0.23 mm to 3.36 +/- 0.03 mm.  Oil globule still present after yolk sac is absorbed; feeding commences at day 15 (24 C) and becomes intensive on day 9 (24 C) or day 14 (22 C) (394).  Silvering begins in abdominal area, spreads dorsally and is complete on day 25 (24 C) when larvae are Ca. 10.9 mm Tl marking end of larval stage (394 438).

Prejuveniles: Duration of stage is temperature dependent lasting from 30 to 90 days with size range of Ca. 11 to 52 mm TL (438 11).  Growth rates in the wild include: 25 mm SL fish in January of class 0 year increasing to 116 mm SL in January of class 1 year; 18 mm SL fish in October increasing to 65 mm SL by mid-April; and 26 mm TL fish increasing to 88 mm TL from February to July (255 294 377).  However, reported growth rates for this and other classes vary widely with climate and other factors (438).  Scales begin forming at about 8 to 10 mm SL and 11 mm TL, and are complete at 12 to 14 mm SL and 17.69 mm TL (11 438 394).  Full number of fin rays formed at about 11.9 mm TL (438).  Fish 20 mm SL weigh 2.3 g (224).  Third anal ray changes to hard spine at 41 to 50 mm TL and marks end of prejuvenile stage (11 438).

Juvenile: Size range of about 44 to 200 mm SL (11 255 438).  Fins same as adult (438).  Caudal fin achieving final form at Ca. 110 mm FL; scales changing suddenly from those of prejuvenile above 30 mm TL, circuli of the posterior (exposed) region becoming complete and less densely packed than those of anterior region.  Lateral stripes generally like adult, becoming increasingly distinct from 44 to 60 mm SL (438).

Adult: Life span for striped mullet is up to 7 yr for males, and 8 yr for females (438 754) with average life span probably ca. 5 yr (294).  Maximum age reported is 13 years (1325).  Broadhead (75) presented data detailing fork length at age for mullet from the Florida west coast.  Females are larger and grow faster than males of the same age (75).  At Crystal River, and Cedar Key, fish >28cm are predominantly females (1330).  Average sizes for size classes 1 through 5 have been recorded in SL as 116 mm, 181 mm, 230 mm, 277 mm, and 324 mm with mean weight increases of 31 g, 84 g, 116 g, and 167 g for first through forth year.(294).  Adults become reproductively mature at 3 years of age or greater when they reach lengths of 200 to 255 mm TL for males and 250 to 350 mm TL for females, or 230 mm to 285 mm FL for males and 243 to 290 mm FL for females (18 74 255 490).  Weight of spawning females ranges 600 to 1400 g (698).  Recorded size range for adults is 20 to 91cm TL; average size usually <50cm TL (377 70 294 224 550 490 561 709 788).  One weight recorded for a 238 mm SL fish was 345.0 g (224).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body:
Larvae: Carnivorous, diet consists of planktonic material (53 279 754). Changes from carnivore to omnivore to herbivore with size increase.  Changeover begins at 15 mm SL and is completed before metamorphosis, usually by 35 mm SL (53 279 754).  Digestion rate increases with body weight, and both digestion and ingestion rates increase with salinity (1321). Diet consists of plant debris, algae (diatoms), copepods (eggs, nauplii, adults), mosquito larvae, and fish residue (279).

Juvenile/Adult: Generally prefer organic detritus, diatoms, filamentous algae, organic matter, benthic organisms, plant tissue, foraminifera, and plankton of correct particle size, but have also been observed with fish scales, sponge spicules, minute gastropods in stomach contents (75 163 301 490 702).  In an IRL wetland impoundment feeding study, over 60% of the diet of mullet by volume was a mixture of algae and detritus while over 30% was sand (1271).  Adults have also been seen actively feeding on a swarm of swimming polychaetes, Nereis succinea (53), and on dinoflagellates (1320).  Termed an iliophagous feeder as diet consists chiefly of bottom surface material and organisms upon which they feed day and night (75 163 301).  Feeding occurs littorally in shallows by sucking up bottom material, straining it through an elaborate pharyngeal sieving mechanism, and jetting filtered material from the gills (75 163 301 702 1329).  Although chiefly herbivorous, mullet may opportunistically feed on animal matter especially in the fall when an above normal protein intake may be required for gonad maturation (53).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
An important forage fish which forms a major component in the flow of energy through the estuarine system by feeding at the lowest trophic levels and providing food to birds, mammals and many important commercial and game fish (220 377 490 967 1317).
Predation: Piscine predators include: Sciaenops ocellatus, Cynoscion nebulosus, Arius felis, Paralichthys lethostigma, Carcharhinus leucas, Lepisosteus spatula, L. osseus Megalops atlanticus (70 163 255 651).
Parasites/Diseases: Parasitic infections are common in mullet, and virtually all adults on the Florida Gulf coast are infected (1317).  A number of parasites have been isolated from mullet including: nematodes, leeches, blood trypanosomes, ciliates, spiny-headed worms, bacteria, protozoa, copepods, and tapeworms (533 537 582).

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title: Striped mullet (Mugil cephalus)

FLELMR Code: 1832

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name: Striped Mullet
Scientific Name: Mugil cephalus

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: Perciformes
	Family: Mugilidae

Other Common Names: Common mullet, black mullet, Biloxi bacon, liza, grey mullet (70 74 116 211 394), jumping mullet (315 834), fatback (315).

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Comprises one of the most important fisheries of the southern United States with total Atlantic mullet landings for 1988 totaling over 32 million pounds (11 513 788).  Since the 1960's, Florida has produced about 80-90% of the US catch.  Statewide Florida landings for 1989 totaled 19,985,200 lbs worth $8,610,461 dockside (average $0.43/lb), of which 17,787,960 lbs were landed at Florida west coast ports (902).  State wide landings of all mullet species combined amounted to 22,798,999 lbs in 1991 (1329).  Striped mullet is considered as both an important food fish especially in Florida where it is also taken for its roe, considered a delicacy, and as a prime species for mariculture (53 116 74).  Florida roe season landings and prices were down from the previous year in 1990_91, but the 1991-92 roe season started strongly in the fall with prices reaching as high as $1.55/lb (1329).  Mullet are caught by gill nets, trammel nets, stop nets, haul seines, yard seines, hook and line, and cast nets (11 74 76 791).  The gill nets and trammel nets are the most effective means of capture with haul and yard seine second in choice.  Hook and line, and cast net catches are incidental.  About 25% is marketed fresh, 63% frozen in the round, 6% smoked, and 6% as roe (1317).

Recreational: Valued as a bait fish by sport fishermen especially for billfish, also indirectly important as an important food source for game fishes (19 377 1317).  Regarded as an excellent food fish (1317).

Indicator: A study by the Environmental Protection Agency has shown that crude oil may serve as a nonspecific stress agent that lowers resistance of mullet to disease (475).  Striped mullet responses to DDT at different temperatures have application for the development of water quality criteria in Australia (570).

Ecological Role: An important forage fish which forms a major component in the flow of energy through the estuarine system by feeding at the lowest trophic levels and providing food to birds, mammals and many important commercial and game fish (220 377 490 967 1317).  Piscine predators include: Sciaenops ocellatus, Cynoscion nebulosus, Arius felis, Paralichthys lethostigma, Carcharhinus leucas, Lepisosteus spatula, L. osseus, Megalops atlanticus (70 163 255 651).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Nearly worldwide in warm waters (788 1316).  In the western Atlantic from Nova Scotia and Bermuda to Santos, Brazil (327 788 891), but most common from the Chesapeake Bay south (1037).  Absent from the West Indies and Caribbean (788).  Found throughout the Gulf of Mexico (891).  Often ascends coastal rivers for considerable distances (790 1037).

Within study area:  Abundant along the Florida coast (1316).  Also occurs in Lake Okeechobee (1313), the St. Lucie, St. Johns and Caloosahatchee Rivers (264 265 1015), and the Big Cypress Swamp and Everglades (395).  It is found throughout the IRL system (848 887 993 264 1242)

Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
All stages are pelagic occurring primarily in the shallow part of the water column although some deep water catches have been reported (18 211 327 438 754).  Larvae are planktonic until 10_12 d from hatching and are then capable of sustained swimming (394).  Prejuveniles, juveniles, and adults are nektonic and form schools ranging from a few individuals up to several hundred (18 19 65 327 377).  Activity related to feeding has been recorded during both day and night (163 301 702).
Movements and Migrations:  One tagging study showed that 91% of the tagged mullet were recovered within 32 km of the release point and only 2% were recovered more than 160 km away (1317).  Later tagging studies, however, reported extensive movements of subadult and adult mullet (>250mm TL) in Florida (1331).  Recaptures ranged from a few km to 500km from the tagging site, and one fish tagged on the Gulf Coast was recaptured in the Atlantic about 210km from the tagging site (1331).  Similar distances have been reported in Australia (1325), and distances of up to 560km have been reported on the east coast of the US (1332).  Schools have been reported to migrate around southern FL from the Atlantic to the Gulf coast (Jacot, 1920 cited in (1322)).  Mullet attain a swimming speed greater than energetically optimal during migration probably due to increased hydromechanical efficiency provided by schooling (1322) suggesting that dispersal can be rapid.

It was thought that Florida Gulf coast populations were divided into at least 3 geographic subpopulations (74 1317).  Recent analysis of electrophoretically detected allozymes was used to describe the genetic structure of Florida mullet populations (1332).  Based on these studies, it was found that striped mullet inhabiting both coasts of Florida essentially represent a single gene pool, and that the earlier speculations and interpretations of population structure could not be supported (1332).

Striped mullet exhibit an inshore-offshore movement in the fall and winter when large schools leave the bays and estuaries in order to spawn in offshore Gulf waters (74 327 481 754).  Tagging studies conducted in the Tampa Bay area indicated that 9 - 17% of tagged mullet emigrated permanently from the bay systems where they were tagged (1315 1316).  Mullet exhibit a preference for bay waters and it has been suggested an organic compound present in these waters may guide mullet back to their native area (390).  Larvae move inshore to shallow waters along beaches and salt marshes (1317), and in Hawaii, schools of mullet <50mm are always found in waters of minimal depth (1319).  Juveniles entering bay systems from offshore waters migrate to nursery areas which are thought to be secondary and tertiary bays and move back to deeper offshore waters as sub-adult to mature and spawn when colder temperatures set in (298).  Movement of mullet is otherwise random and usually restricted to a broad coastal area (74 75 76 481).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type: One of the most abundant fishes in shallow Gulf waters usually with highest biomass (294). They are most abundant in waters near shore occupying virtually all shallow marine and estuarine habitats including open beaches, flats, lagoons, bays, rivers, salt marshes, and grass beds (70 103 116 255 294 298 224 255 377 550 490 588 664 694).  Eggs and larvae occupy an offshore marine habitat where they undergo early development and as prejuveniles enter the bays and estuaries to mature when 15 to 32 mm TL from November to June with the greatest concentration from December to February (255 588 294 322 224 550 694 116 696 305 709 754 510).  In some instances, females greatly outnumber males in brackish and freshwater habitats (1323 1329).  Reported from fresh to hypersaline waters and from waters with depths of a few centimeters to 1385 m appearing to prefer <3 (18 70 103 116 140 211 255 264 265 298 395 438 490 550 561 651 694 754 790).

Substrate: Prefer softer sediments such as mud and sand which contain decaying organic detritus, but also occur over finely ground shell, clay, mud and sand mixtures, silt, and silt-clay mixtures (70 140 224 377 694 702 754).  Striped mullet also frequent grass beds of Thallasia especially at night (53 298 786) and have also been observed around patches of Ruppia (224).

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content:
Egg: Egg development has been recorded over a range of 10 to 31.9 C in both laboratory and field observations with the optimum range occurring at 21 to 24 C (211 394 501 698 699 754).
Larvae: Development possible from 15.9 to 29.1 C with optimum growth and survival occurring at 20 to 22 C (394 501 698 754).  Survival and growth over a broad thermal range despite temperatures at spawning sites probably varying very little may be a preadaptation to accommodate temperatures changes as the larvae sink vertically through the water (698).
Prejuveniles occur at temperatures of 5.0 C up to a maximum exceeding 30 C (116 438 754).
Juveniles/Adults: Appear able to adjust to a wide range of temperatures (70 754).  Not a permanent resident in waters with temperatures below 16 C or where water temperatures don't reach 18 C (1317).  Recorded collections from 5.9 to 37.0 C but the ability to withstand short periods of 40 C has been observed (255 377 294 224 550 694 193 490 561 709 754).  Collected in Tampa Bay at temperatures of 10.7 - 32.5 C (664).  Preference temperatures are 20 to 30 C for juveniles and >16 to 30 C for adults (754).

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content:
Eggs: Spawning and development have occurred at 28 to 36.5 ppt with optimum survival occurring at 30 to 33 ppt (211 394 698 754).  Eggs have much less tolerance to salinity variation than larvae, but a greater tolerance to sea water (698).

Larvae: Stenohaline at hatching becoming increasingly euryhaline with increasing size (510).  Able to tolerate salinities ranging from 16 to 36.5 ppt with reported optimal ranges being 32 to 33 ppt and 26 to 28 ppt (211 394 510 698 754).  Prejuveniles recorded from a range of 0 to 54 ppt with a preference for <1 to 40 ppt (116 255 694 754).

Juvenile/Adult: Both stages euryhaline with similar tolerances; observed in salinities ranging from 0.0 to 75 ppt, but  adults appear to prefer median salinities of approximately 26 ppt  and juveniles range from 20 to 28 ppt (255 377 651 321 588 294 550 193 116 696 561 709 211 754 140).  Taken in Tampa Bay at salinities ranging from 0 to 35 ppt (664).

Other: Eggs and larvae prefer higher concentrations of oxygen (>4.0 ppm) and are not able to tolerate ranges as low as juveniles and adults can (103 754).  Larvae apparently cannot survive in dissolved oxygen concentrations below 4 ppm (1324).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: Sexual, gonochoristic, polygamous, oviparous, broadcast spawners with external fertilization.

Mating/Spawning: Spawning begins in October, peaked in November-December, and ends in March (65 255 74 582 11 18 75 19 116 751 490 614 206 211 754).  Some females in Australia spawn only in alternate years (1325), and there is evidence that this may also be true for US waters (1323).  Ripe mullet collect in passes in large schools and migrate offshore with return of spent adults beginning 10 days later and continuing until May (18 255 327 490 614 1315 1316).  Spawning takes place in offshore marine waters of the Gulf of Mexico over a broad area of the continental shelf (11 18 211 298 510).  Spawners occur in small groups of 3 to 6 fish swimming close to the surface in an erratic manner (18).  Males would stay slightly behind a single female pressing against her and from time to time would visibly quiver (18 65).  No direct evidence on spawning salinities and temperatures is available, but spawning is apparently unsuccessful at low salinities (116 438).  Hormonal and natural spawning in the laboratory was best induced at 23.8 to 23.5 C and 21 C respectively (394 698) in salinities ranging from 30 to 32 ppt (394 501 698).

Fecundity: Fecundity has been estimated in laboratory studies as being 648 +/- 62 (501) to 849 +/- 62 eggs/g body weight (640) with recorded releases ranging from 0.76 to 7.2 million eggs/female (438 754).  Another study estimated fecundity is 0.5 to 2.0 million eggs/female, depending on the size of the female (74).  Fertilization rates in the laboratory have ranged from 53 to 95 % (394 501 640).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg: Non-adhesive, spherical, transparent to straw colored (438 754).  Sizes range in diameter from 0.88 to 0.94 mm and average 0.93 to 0.95 mm (211 394 501 640 698).  Characterized by a single large oil globule with a uniform diameter ranging 0.30 to 0.36 mm and averaging 0.33 mm (211 394 501).  First cleavage occurs 50 to 65 min after fertilization (AF) at 22 C; blastula stage is reached at 5 hr and 40 min AF at 24 C followed by the gastrula stage 7 hr 35 min AF (394 501).  By 13 hr 30 min AF the neurula stage occurs characterized by the appearance of the neural groove and is followed by optic vesicle development, tail expansion, somatic segmentation, and differentiation of olfactory lobes (394).  Heart beat begins 25 h 10 min AF and body movement evident at 27 h AF (394).  Incubation period is 36 to 38 hrs AF at 24 C and 48 to 50 hrs at 22 C (394 501).

Larvae: TL at hatching is 2.1 mm to 2.88 mm TL with a reported average of 2.65 +/- 0.23 mm TL (211 394 501 698).  At hatching yolk sac ovoid or oblong ellipsoidal with oil globule near center or rear of yolk sac (438).  Mouth opens on day 2 to 3; larval are independently active; eyes sufficiently pigmented for food finding; yolk sac is absorbed by day 5 (24 C) (394 501 754).  Most growth during yolksac stage occurs during day 1 with larval TL's increasing from 2.65 +/-0.23 mm to 3.36 +/- 0.03 mm.  Oil globule still present after yolk sac is absorbed; feeding commences at day 15 (24 C) and becomes intensive on day 9 (24 C) or day 14 (22 C) (394).  Silvering begins in abdominal area, spreads dorsally and is complete on day 25 (24 C) when larvae are Ca. 10.9 mm Tl marking end of larval stage (394 438).

Prejuveniles: Duration of stage is temperature dependent lasting from 30 to 90 days with size range of Ca. 11 to 52 mm TL (438 11).  Growth rates in the wild include: 25 mm SL fish in January of class 0 year increasing to 116 mm SL in January of class 1 year; 18 mm SL fish in October increasing to 65 mm SL by mid-April; and 26 mm TL fish increasing to 88 mm TL from February to July (255 294 377).  However, reported growth rates for this and other classes vary widely with climate and other factors (438).  Scales begin forming at about 8 to 10 mm SL and 11 mm TL, and are complete at 12 to 14 mm SL and 17.69 mm TL (11 438 394).  Full number of fin rays formed at about 11.9 mm TL (438).  Fish 20 mm SL weigh 2.3 g (224).  Third anal ray changes to hard spine at 41 to 50 mm TL and marks end of prejuvenile stage (11 438).

Juvenile: Size range of about 44 to 200 mm SL (11 255 438).  Fins same as adult (438).  Caudal fin achieving final form at Ca. 110 mm FL; scales changing suddenly from those of prejuvenile above 30 mm TL, circuli of the posterior (exposed) region becoming complete and less densely packed than those of anterior region.  Lateral stripes generally like adult, becoming increasingly distinct from 44 to 60 mm SL (438).

Adult: Life span for striped mullet is up to 7 yr for males, and 8 yr for females (438 754) with average life span probably ca. 5 yr (294).  Maximum age reported is 13 years (1325).  Broadhead (75) presented data detailing fork length at age for mullet from the Florida west coast.  Females are larger and grow faster than males of the same age (75).  At Crystal River, and Cedar Key, fish >28cm are predominantly females (1330).  Average sizes for size classes 1 through 5 have been recorded in SL as 116 mm, 181 mm, 230 mm, 277 mm, and 324 mm with mean weight increases of 31 g, 84 g, 116 g, and 167 g for first through forth year.(294).  Adults become reproductively mature at 3 years of age or greater when they reach lengths of 200 to 255 mm TL for males and 250 to 350 mm TL for females, or 230 mm to 285 mm FL for males and 243 to 290 mm FL for females (18 74 255 490).  Weight of spawning females ranges 600 to 1400 g (698).  Recorded size range for adults is 20 to 91cm TL; average size usually <50cm TL (377 70 294 224 550 490 561 709 788).  One weight recorded for a 238 mm SL fish was 345.0 g (224).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content:
Larvae: Carnivorous, diet consists of planktonic material (53 279 754). Changes from carnivore to omnivore to herbivore with size increase.  Changeover begins at 15 mm SL and is completed before metamorphosis, usually by 35 mm SL (53 279 754).  Digestion rate increases with body weight, and both digestion and ingestion rates increase with salinity (1321). Diet consists of plant debris, algae (diatoms), copepods (eggs, nauplii, adults), mosquito larvae, and fish residue (279).

Juvenile/Adult: Generally prefer organic detritus, diatoms, filamentous algae, organic matter, benthic organisms, plant tissue, foraminifera, and plankton of correct particle size, but have also been observed with fish scales, sponge spicules, minute gastropods in stomach contents (75 163 301 490 702).  In an IRL wetland impoundment feeding study, over 60% of the diet of mullet by volume was a mixture of algae and detritus while over 30% was sand (1271).  Adults have also been seen actively feeding on a swarm of swimming polychaetes, Nereis succinea (53), and on dinoflagellates (1320).  Termed an iliophagous feeder as diet consists chiefly of bottom surface material and organisms upon which they feed day and night (75 163 301).  Feeding occurs littorally in shallows by sucking up bottom material, straining it through an elaborate pharyngeal sieving mechanism, and jetting filtered material from the gills (75 163 301 702 1329).  Although chiefly herbivorous, mullet may opportunistically feed on animal matter especially in the fall when an above normal protein intake may be required for gonad maturation (53).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
An important forage fish which forms a major component in the flow of energy through the estuarine system by feeding at the lowest trophic levels and providing food to birds, mammals and many important commercial and game fish (220 377 490 967 1317).
Predation: Piscine predators include: Sciaenops ocellatus, Cynoscion nebulosus, Arius felis, Paralichthys lethostigma, Carcharhinus leucas, Lepisosteus spatula, L. osseus Megalops atlanticus (70 163 255 651).
Parasites/Diseases: Parasitic infections are common in mullet, and virtually all adults on the Florida Gulf coast are infected (1317).  A number of parasites have been isolated from mullet including: nematodes, leeches, blood trypanosomes, ciliates, spiny-headed worms, bacteria, protozoa, copepods, and tapeworms (533 537 582).
